To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Australian universities agree on the importance of assessment that is: 1) aligned with learning outcomes and course objectives; 2) valid, reliable and fair; 3) authentic; 4) timely and frequent feedback; 5) clear and consistent marking criteria; 6) transparent; 7) engaging; 8) flexible; 9) supportive and encouraging; 10) fair; 11) inclusive and accessible; 12) formative; and 13) authentic.

the universities in our sample are generally in agreement about good assessment practices and that the most important principles are that assessment should: • be authentic • be fair and equitable • be valid, reliable, and consistent • be timely and efficient • be formative as well as summative • be designed to engage students in their learning • provide feedback • be transparent • be consistent with the learning objectives • be consistent with professional and/or disciplinary standards • be consistent with university and institutional requirements.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of Australian universities are committed to the principles of good assessment practice, but that there is a significant minority who do not share that commitment.
Australian universities have a good understanding of the principles of good assessment practice and have a good grasp of the principles of engaging assessment.
the majority of Australian universities are in agreement with the principles of assessment practice as espoused by the international community.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the universities are in broad agreement with the mainstream principles.

there is a clear consensus on what good assessment should look like, and that there is a significant degree of support for the principles of authentic assessment, assessment for learning, and student engagement.

the majority of universities agree on the importance of a small set of principles, and the importance of these principles is not in doubt, but the degree of support for these principles is not as high as it could be.
